trim the base64 in the first javascript to reveal a powershell payload

the powershell writes an executable file un the user's music directory

```
> file ./stage3.exe
./stage3.exe: PE32 executable (GUI) Intel 80386 Mono/.Net assembly, for MS Windows
```

neither ghidra or binary ninja can seem to analyze the code flow properly, but if we take a look at data, we can find [some hints](https://cyberchef.formality.de/#recipe=From_Hex('Auto')Remove_null_bytes()&&oeol=CRLF) , unfortunately nothing very readable

if we use a dedicated .NET decompiler like [ILSpy](https://github.com/icsharpcode/ILSpy) we can find some interesting info in the `UltraSpeed` namespace:

```

{

UltraSpeed.StrSignature = "\r\n***********************************************************\r\n* *\r\n* *\r\n* _ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ *\r\n* Best | | / _ \\ / __|/ __| __| _ \\ *\r\n* | |_| (_) | (_ | (_ | _|| / *\r\n* Private - - - -> |____\\___/ \\___|\\___|___|_|_\\ *\r\n* *\r\n* *\r\n* *\r\n***********************************************************";
```

the interesting bit is `UltraSpeed.TG_Access = "8485770488:AAH8YOjqaRckDPIy7xNwZN2KcaLx6EME-L0";` which seems to be a telegram bot api key (and it fits with the challenge's prompt), let's dig further first by using existing resources like [this blog post](https://polygonben.github.io/malware%20analysis/Compromising-Threat-Actor-Communications/)

using the [mentioned script](https://github.com/anyrun/blog-scripts/blob/main/Scripts/TelegramAPI/prepare_bot.py) we can get some info on the bot:

```
❯ uv run python prepare_bot.py 8485770488:AAH8YOjqaRckDPIy7xNwZN2KcaLx6EME-L0

Use this data to find bot in Telegram:
Bot username: st38l3r_bot
Bot title: st3aler
```
